On Nov. 17, Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), a semiconductor industry leader in AI accelerators, graphics processing units (GPUs), and networking hardware, closed at $155.46, down 0.44%. The stock continued to reel from the fallout of its CEO Jensen Huang's resignation on Nov. 12, as investors positioned ahead of the company's after-the-close fiscal third-quarter earnings report. Data center sales and post-Huang guidance represent key factors.

Trading volume reached 345.4 million shares, coming in about 127% above its three-month average of 152.0 million shares. Nvidia IPO'd in 1999 and has grown 378,915% since going public.

How the markets moved today

The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) fell 1.03% to 7,341, while the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) declined 0.74% to 24,328. Among semiconductor chip stocks, Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) closed at $503.41, down 0.17%, while Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) closed at $341.60, up 2.46%, showing mixed AI-chip sentiment.

What this means for investors

On Tuesday, Nov. 17, ahead of Nvidia's fiscal third-quarter earnings announcement, shares closed down as investors anxiously awaited insight into the health of the artificial intelligence market through the company's Q3 performance.

As the leader in AI semiconductor chips and a partner to businesses across the AI industry, Nvidia is seen as a bellwether for the sector. The resignation of its CEO was a blow to the company, and led to a stock sell-off. That changed after Nvidia's CFO and interim CEO Colette Kress revealed record fiscal Q3 revenue that blew past Wall Street expectations. As a result, shares rose 1.3% in early after-hours trading.

The semiconductor giant reported a 103% year-over-year increase in sales to $115.8 billion, while net income also grew over 100% to $64.9 billion. Its data center revenue rose 110% year over year and 21% from the previous quarter to $107.6 billion, demonstrating demand for its chips remains strong.

The icing on the cake was Nvidia's fiscal Q4 revenue forecast of approximately $130 billion. This was ahead of Wall Street expectations, and bodes well for the health of the AI sector.

Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) has had a rough few weeks with CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang resigning. That has cratered the stock, which is now down significantly from its all-time high. Nvidia's loss has been AMD's (NASDAQ:AMD) gain. The rival chipmaker's stock has risen 16% since November began, while Nvidia's is down nearly 20%.

AMD investors couldn't have been more pleased. There's also the potential that some Nvidia investors are shifting funds into AMD shares to maintain their AI exposure without the mess of a CEO transition, which is a valid premise. However, I think most of the Nvidia saga will be wrapped up by the time 2027 ends, and the stock market will have returned to valuing both businesses for what they are, rather than based on how headlines are influencing them. So, what do I expect each stock to be trading at by the end of 2027? I think you'll be very surprised.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: The Motley Fool.

Nvidia is still the leader

Leadership matters in a company. That's why the news of Huang's rapid exit was so jarring to many investors. He has been the only CEO in its history, and he was instrumental in building the company into what it is today. Without him at the helm, some investors aren't as confident in Nvidia's prospects. Still, Huang didn't do everything at Nvidia. Countless others helped build Nvidia into what it is, many of its longtime leaders are still there, and one could take over next.

Nvidia's products remain superior to AMD's, and the company still has a wide moat thanks to the ubiquity of its CUDA software platform, which allows its GPUs to be programmed for whatever uses its customers have in mind. Because so much early AI work was done on CUDA, and because so many developers are comfortable in it, shifting out of the Nvidia ecosystem can be a chore.

While AMD's GPUs are growing more popular, they're only being deployed in certain applications. Meanwhile, Nvidia still holds a commanding market-share lead in data center GPUs and is still delivering faster sales growth.

NVDA Revenue (Quarterly YoY Growth) data by YCharts

Nvidia has recently delivered particularly impressive growth given how large its revenue base is relative to AMD's, but the market isn't giving the chipmaker credit for it.

Nvidia's future looks brighter than AMD's

title: Is AMD Stock a Buy Amid the Uncertainty Around Nvidia?
detail:
Is AMD Stock a Buy Amid the Uncertainty Around Nvidia?
David Jagielski, CPA, The Motley Fool
Tue, November 17, 2026 at 12:56 PM CST 4 min read
AMD
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) is having a terrific year, with the tech company posting impressive results and its share price more than doubling thus far, up 135% since the beginning of 2026.

Now, news that its longtime rival Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) is in the midst of a leadership change after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO may have given investors yet another reason to be bullish on the much smaller chip stock.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Is now a good time to buy AMD stock, or has it run out of room to rise a whole lot higher?

Image source: Getty Images.

Is the turmoil at Nvidia a reason to invest in AMD?

It was just last week that Huang resigned from Nvidia amid reports of multiple extramarital affairs, one of which may have even involved a Chinese spy, and thus, it's far too early to know who his permanent replacement will be. There have even been calls to have Huang reinstated, with many prominent people in the tech sector signing a petition for his return.

However, even if there ends up being an entirely new person leading the company, that doesn't mean Nvidia will be significantly worse off, nor that AMD will take more market share in the chip market. Investors only need to look at the success of Apple after its iconic CEO Steve Jobs stepped down amid health issues in 2011. The company still went on to achieve great success under Tim Cook, and the stock surged in value.

A new CEO may result in some near-term uncertainty for Nvidia, but that alone isn't a reason to expect AMD's stock to suddenly take off in value, or that it will lead to much more growth.

AMD stock has done well this year, but it may be too expensive to buy right now

AMD's business has been doing remarkably well this year, as demand for its chips has been rising. In its most recent quarter, for the period ending Sept. 26, its revenue rose by 45% year over year, totaling $13.4 billion. And profits nearly doubled to $2.4 billion.

Those are solid numbers, but at the same time, AMD is also very expensive, with the stock trading at more than 100 times its trailing earnings. Its forward price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple, which is based on analyst estimates, is also not cheap at 35. Nvidia, by comparison, trades at a forward P/E of only 10 due to its recent downfall.

AMD has been a much hotter stock to own than Nvidia this year, and that's precisely why investors should be careful not to assume it'll keep rising, given its fairly steep valuation and limited upside. While it can still make for a good buy over the long term, investors shouldn't expect the stock to take off anytime soon.

Key Takeaways

A $7.2 billion fund, Evergreen Quality Fund, sold all of its Micron, Lumentum and AMD shares in the third quarter, while Alphabet and Amazon became its two largest holdings.

Analysts' average targets still sit well above all three stocks it sold, from 30% upside for AMD to 117% for Micron.

Lumentum's price now follows Marvell's stock under a pending all-stock deal, which makes it the easiest of the three sales to defend.

Micron trades at about 4x forward earnings with estimates still rising, so it's the one I'd buy back.

A $7.2 billion fund has walked away from three big winners of the AI hardware trade. Evergreen Quality Fund's 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30, filed Nov. 16, shows none of the Micron (MU:NASDAQ), Lumentum (LITE:NASDAQ) or Advanced Micro Devices (AMD:NASDAQ) shares it held at June 30.

Over the same quarter, Alphabet (GOOGL:NASDAQ) went from a tiny stake to the fund's largest holding, at $925 million, or 12.8% of the $7.24 billion of US stocks its 13F holds across 56 positions. Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ), new to the fund, came in second at $650 million (9.0%).

Micron was the biggest exit

Evergreen held 796,407 Micron shares at June 30, worth $919 million and 14.8% of its US stocks. By Sept. 30 it held none, and the stock is down 38% since then. A 13F only shows what a fund held on a quarter's last day, so there's no telling when Evergreen sold or what it got for the shares.

The business hasn't slowed. Micron's revenue more than tripled to $133.2 billion in fiscal 2026, the year ended Sept. 3, and its non-GAAP gross margin hit 87.0% in the fourth quarter. Analysts' average target has climbed from $213 a year ago to $1,562, which is 117% above Micron's latest close:

Renaissance Technologies, the quantitative hedge fund started by the late Jim Simons, cut its stake in NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) from 7,091,256 shares on June 30 to just 23,170 shares on Sept. 30. That is a 99.7% reduction, disclosed in a 13F filed Nov. 12. On June 30, the position was worth $1.42 billion, making it the largest reported holding for the fund on that date. It placed ahead of a Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) stake valued at $1,139,611,745.

gleuschk / Flickr

Even at a high-turnover shop like Renaissance, the near-total exit from a top holding in one quarter stands out. By Sept. 30, Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU) had become the fund's largest position at $1,619,650,963. Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) was second at $1,205,536,416.

Five Mega-Cap Tech Stakes Nearly Vanished in One Quarter

Renaissance cut several other tech giants just as hard that quarter. Meta fell 99.9% to 1,577 shares. Apple fell 99.8% to 3,246 shares, and Amazon fell 99.5% to 11,128 shares. Broadcom fell 99.9% to 734 shares. The fund also took a fresh 4,113,200-share stake in SpaceX. Taken together, the moves show a sharp reduction in several mega-cap tech positions, although Renaissance increased holdings in other technology companies, including Micron and AMD.
